name: Linear Algebra Basics
author: Recurse
subject: math
description: Vectors, dot products, matrix multiplication, transformations, determinants, inverses and linear systems.

lesson.intro: Linear algebra studies vectors and the transformations that move them. It powers computer graphics, machine learning and physics simulations, and it turns a whole system of equations into a single matrix problem.

sections.title: Vectors
sections.body:
A vector is a quantity with size and direction, written as a list of components. The vector v = (3, 4) means 3 units along x and 4 units along y. Vectors can have any number of components; (1, −2, 5) lives in 3D space.

- Addition is componentwise: (1, 2) + (3, −1) = (4, 1). Geometrically, place the second arrow at the tip of the first
- Scalar multiplication multiplies every component: 2(3, 4) = (6, 8) is twice as long, and −1(3, 4) = (−3, −4) points the opposite way
- Subtraction: u − v = u + (−1)v

The length (magnitude) of a vector comes from the Pythagorean theorem: ‖(3, 4)‖ = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. In 3D, add the third component's square under the root.

A unit vector has length 1. Divide any nonzero vector by its length to get the unit vector pointing the same way: (3, 4)/5 = (0.6, 0.8).

A linear combination of u and v is a·u + b·v for numbers a and b. Every vector in the plane is a linear combination of (1, 0) and (0, 1): (3, 4) = 3(1, 0) + 4(0, 1).

check.question: What is 3(1, −2) − (2, 1)?
check.explanation: Scale first: 3(1, −2) = (3, −6). Then subtract componentwise: (3 − 2, −6 − 1) = (1, −7). (1, −5) adds the 1 instead of subtracting it.

sections.title: The dot product and angles
sections.body:
The dot product multiplies matching components and adds the results. The answer is a single number, not a vector:

u · v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂ + ...

For example, (1, 2, 3) · (4, −5, 6) = 4 − 10 + 18 = 12.

Geometrically, the dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way:

u · v = ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ

where θ is the angle between them. Rearranged, cos θ = (u · v) / (‖u‖ ‖v‖), which lets you find any angle from components alone.

- Positive dot product: the angle is less than 90°
- Zero: exactly 90°; the vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular)
- Negative: the angle is greater than 90°

A vector dotted with itself gives its length squared: v · v = ‖v‖². Checking for a zero dot product is the standard test for perpendicular vectors.

check.question: Are (2, 3) and (3, −2) perpendicular?
choices: No, because their dot product is 12
No, because one component is negative
Yes, because they have the same length
Yes, because their dot product is 0
check.explanation: (2)(3) + (3)(−2) = 6 − 6 = 0, so they are perpendicular. Equal length happens to be true here but is not the test: (3, 4) and (4, 3) have equal lengths and are not perpendicular. 12 comes from dropping the minus sign.

sections.title: Matrices and matrix multiplication
sections.body:
A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers. An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. In this pack we write matrices row by row: [[1, 2], [3, 4]] has first row 1, 2 and second row 3, 4.

To multiply A by B, the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. An m × n matrix times an n × p matrix gives an m × p matrix. The entry in row i, column j of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.

Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB and BA are usually different, and when the shapes do not match, one of them may not even exist. The example below shows two 2 × 2 matrices whose products differ. The order is part of the meaning.

The identity matrix I has 1s on the main diagonal and 0s everywhere else, such as [[1, 0], [0, 1]]. It plays the role of the number 1: AI = IA = A for any square matrix A of matching size.

check.question: A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 4. What is the size of AB?
check.explanation: The inner sizes match (3 and 3), so AB exists, and its size comes from the outer sizes: 2 rows from A and 4 columns from B. BA, on the other hand, is not defined, because 4 ≠ 2.

sections.title: Linear transformations and determinants
sections.body:
A matrix is also a function: it takes a vector x and returns Ax. These functions are linear transformations. They keep the origin fixed, keep straight lines straight and evenly spaced, and satisfy A(u + v) = Au + Av and A(cv) = c(Av).

The easiest way to read a 2 × 2 matrix: its first column is where (1, 0) lands, and its second column is where (0, 1) lands. Everything else follows by linearity.

- [[2, 0], [0, 2]] scales everything by 2
- [[0, −1], [1, 0]] rotates 90° counterclockwise
- [[1, 0], [0, −1]] reflects across the x-axis

Applying B first and then A is the single matrix AB (read right to left), which is another reason order matters.

The determinant of [[a, b], [c, d]] is ad − bc. It is the factor by which the transformation scales areas: a determinant of 3 triples every area. A negative determinant also flips orientation, like a mirror. A determinant of 0 squashes the plane onto a line or a single point, which loses information.
sections.code:
R = [0 −1]     rotate 90° counterclockwise
    [1  0]
R(1, 0) = (0, 1)      R(0, 1) = (−1, 0)
det R = 0·0 − (−1)(1) = 1      areas unchanged

check.question: What is the determinant of [[3, 1], [2, 4]]?
check.explanation: ad − bc = 3·4 − 1·2 = 12 − 2 = 10. 14 adds the two products instead of subtracting, and 12 forgets the bc term.

sections.title: Inverses and systems of equations
sections.body:
The inverse of a square matrix A, written A⁻¹, undoes it: A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I. If A rotates by 90° counterclockwise, A⁻¹ rotates 90° back.

An inverse exists exactly when det A ≠ 0. A determinant of 0 means different inputs were squashed onto the same output, and nothing can separate them again. For a 2 × 2 matrix:

[[a, b], [c, d]]⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc)) · [[d, −b], [−c, a]]

In words: swap a and d, negate b and c, and divide everything by the determinant.

A system of linear equations is a single matrix equation Ax = b. The system 2x + y = 5 and x − y = 1 has A = [[2, 1], [1, −1]] and b = (5, 1). When det A ≠ 0 there is exactly one solution, x = A⁻¹b. Small systems are usually solved by elimination, as below.

With two unknowns, each equation is a line, so there are three possibilities:

- The lines cross once: exactly one solution (det A ≠ 0)
- The lines are parallel: no solution
- The lines are the same line: infinitely many solutions
sections.code:
2x + y = 5
 x − y = 1
Add the equations:   3x = 6       →   x = 2
Substitute:          2 − y = 1    →   y = 1

check.question: Which matrix has no inverse?
check.explanation: det [[2, 4], [1, 2]] = 2·2 − 4·1 = 0, so it squashes the plane onto a line and cannot be undone. The other three have determinants 1, 3 and −1, all nonzero.

keyTerms.definition: A quantity with size and direction, written as a list of components such as (3, 4).
u · v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂ + ..., a single number equal to ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ.
Perpendicular; two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is 0.
Combining an m × n and an n × p matrix into an m × p matrix; each entry is a row of the first dotted with a column of the second.
The square matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere; AI = IA = A.
A function on vectors that preserves addition and scaling; every matrix defines one.
For [[a, b], [c, d]], the number ad − bc: the factor by which the transformation scales area.
The matrix A⁻¹ with A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I; it exists only when det A ≠ 0.

summary: Vectors add componentwise and scale by multiplying every component; length is the square root of the sum of squares.
The dot product is a number: zero means perpendicular, and u · v = ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ gives the angle.
Each entry of AB is a row of A dotted with a column of B, and AB usually differs from BA.
A matrix is a linear transformation; its determinant is the area scale factor, and det = 0 means there is no inverse.
A system Ax = b has exactly one solution when det A ≠ 0, namely x = A⁻¹b.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why putting on socks and then shoes is different from shoes and then socks, and connect that to why AB and BA are usually different matrices.

questions.question: What is the length of the vector (6, 8)?
questions.explanation: ‖(6, 8)‖ = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. Adding the components (to get 14) is a common slip; length uses squares and a square root.

questions.question: What is (2, −1, 4) + (−3, 5, 0)?
questions.explanation: Add matching components: (2 − 3, −1 + 5, 4 + 0) = (−1, 4, 4). (5, −6, 4) subtracts instead of adding, and (−6, −5, 0) multiplies matching components.

questions.question: Which is the unit vector in the direction of (5, 12)?
questions.explanation: The length is √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13, so the unit vector is (5/13, 12/13). Dividing by 17, the sum of the components, gives a vector shorter than 1.

questions.question: Compute (2, −1, 3) · (4, 0, −2).
questions.explanation: 2·4 + (−1)·0 + 3·(−2) = 8 + 0 − 6 = 2. The dot product is a single number, not the vector (8, 0, −6).

questions.question: For what value of k are (k, 2) and (3, −6) perpendicular?
questions.explanation: Perpendicular means the dot product is 0: 3k + 2(−6) = 3k − 12 = 0, so k = 4. Check: (4, 2) · (3, −6) = 12 − 12 = 0.

questions.question: What is the angle, in degrees, between (1, 0) and (−1, √3)?
questions.explanation: The dot product is −1. The lengths are 1 and √(1 + 3) = 2. cos θ = −1/2, so θ = 120°. A negative dot product always means an angle over 90°, which rules out 60°.

questions.question: What does the dot product of two vectors tell you geometrically?
questions.answer: How much they point in the same direction. It equals ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ, so it is positive when the angle is under 90°, zero when the vectors are perpendicular, and negative when the angle is over 90°.
questions.explanation: cos θ is 1 at 0°, 0 at 90° and −1 at 180°, so the dot product turns a question about angles into simple arithmetic on components. That is why a zero dot product is the test for perpendicular vectors.

questions.question: A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]] and B = [[1, 0], [3, 1]]. What is AB?
questions.explanation: Row 1 of A with the columns of B: (1, 2)·(1, 3) = 7 and (1, 2)·(0, 1) = 2. Row 2: (0, 1)·(1, 3) = 3 and (0, 1)·(0, 1) = 1. [[1, 2], [3, 7]] is BA, and [[1, 0], [0, 1]] comes from multiplying matching entries, which is not matrix multiplication.

questions.question: A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]. What is the entry in row 2, column 1 of AB?
questions.explanation: Row 2 of A is (3, 4) and column 1 of B is (5, 7). Their dot product is 3·5 + 4·7 = 15 + 28 = 43. Multiplying matching entries would give 3·7 = 21, which is not how matrix products work.

questions.question: Which statement about multiplying two square matrices A and B of the same size is true?
choices: AB and BA can be different
AB equals BA whenever both are 2 × 2
AB is found by multiplying matching entries
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Rotating a shape and then reflecting it usually gives a different result from reflecting first, and the matrices AB and BA record that difference.

questions.question: The matrix [[0, −1], [1, 0]] rotates vectors 90° counterclockwise. Where does it send (2, 1)?
questions.explanation: Row 1 · (2, 1) = 0·2 + (−1)·1 = −1. Row 2 · (2, 1) = 1·2 + 0·1 = 2. The result is (−1, 2), a quarter turn counterclockwise. (1, −2) is the clockwise rotation.

questions.question: What is the determinant of [[4, 3], [2, 5]]?
questions.explanation: ad − bc = 4·5 − 3·2 = 20 − 6 = 14, so this transformation multiplies every area by 14. Computing 4·5 + 3·2 = 26 is the usual sign mistake.

questions.question: Which matrix sends (1, 0) to (2, 1) and (0, 1) to (−1, 3)?
questions.explanation: The columns of a matrix are the images of (1, 0) and (0, 1). Column 1 is (2, 1) and column 2 is (−1, 3), so written row by row the matrix is [[2, −1], [1, 3]]. [[2, 1], [−1, 3]] puts the images in the rows instead of the columns.

questions.question: What does a determinant of 0 mean geometrically?
questions.answer: The transformation squashes space into a lower dimension, such as flattening the plane onto a line, so every area becomes 0. Different inputs land on the same output, so the transformation cannot be undone and the matrix has no inverse.
questions.explanation: [[1, 2], [2, 4]] sends every vector onto the line y = 2x, because its second column is twice its first. Its determinant is 1·4 − 2·2 = 0.

questions.question: Solve the system x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. What is x?
questions.explanation: Add the equations: 2x = 14, so x = 7. Then y = 10 − 7 = 3. Check: 7 + 3 = 10 and 7 − 3 = 4.

questions.question: What is the inverse of [[2, 1], [5, 3]]?
questions.explanation: det = 2·3 − 1·5 = 1. Swap a and d, negate b and c, and divide by 1: [[3, −1], [−5, 2]]. Check the top-left entry of the product: 2·3 + 1·(−5) = 1. Taking the reciprocal of each entry does not give an inverse.

questions.question: How many solutions does the system 2x + 4y = 6 and x + 2y = 5 have?
questions.explanation: Dividing the first equation by 2 gives x + 2y = 3, which contradicts x + 2y = 5. The lines are parallel, so there is no solution. The determinant 2·2 − 4·1 = 0 already warns that there is not exactly one solution; the equations decide between none and infinitely many.
